question.text: Assertion: Suppose reference frames S₁ and S₂ are both non-inertial; then an observer in S₁ would find S₂ to be an inertial frame. Reason: A frame being in motion does not by itself make it non-inertial.

options.1: both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.2: both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion
options.3: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false
options.4: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

conditions: S₁ and S₂ are both non-inertial frames

solution.approach: Check whether the relative acceleration of S₂ with respect to S₁ must vanish merely because both are non-inertial, then judge the general truth of the Reason on its own.

steps.text: A frame is non-inertial only if it has some acceleration relative to an inertial (ground) frame; being non-inertial is about acceleration, not about motion in general.
Viewed from S₁, the relative acceleration of S₂ is the difference of their accelerations relative to the ground.
steps.equation: a(S₂ relative to S₁) = a(S₂) − a(S₁)

steps.text: This difference is zero only in the special case that S₁ and S₂ happen to share the same acceleration, which is not stated here, so in general S₂ stays non-inertial even when viewed from S₁ — the Assertion is false as a general claim.
steps.equation: a(S₂) − a(S₁) ≠ 0 in general ⇒ Assertion false

steps.text: The Reason is a true, separate statement: a frame moving at constant velocity is still inertial, so mere motion does not make a frame non-inertial — only acceleration does.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming that viewing one non-inertial frame from another non-inertial frame always cancels out the acceleration completely, making S₂ look inertial from S₁ in every case, and picking both statements true.
